data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

A machine cannot give you something for nothing. Every one of them makes the same trade, and once you see it you cannot unsee it.

1. Read **The Deal** — the last paragraph is the point of the whole lesson.
2. Learn the six machines in the **Glossary**, then win the **Matching** game and the **Bingo** game.
3. Keep the **Six Machines** chart open while you look around the room.
4. Sort the objects in **Which Machine Is It?** — two of them are arguments.
5. Take the quiz. Question 4 asks about the trade, which is the real idea.
6. Use the **Sentence Frames** to explain a machine you actually use.
7. Lock the ideas in with **Remember the Six Machines** — study the example aid, then make one your own.
8. Finish with **Design Challenge: Lift the Water Jug** — use what you learned on a real problem, and mark every guess as a guess.
9. Study the **Six Machines, Two Families** before the sort — the six machines fall into just two families.

Challenge while you work: find five simple machines in the room you are sitting in right now. There are more than you think. ⚙️

Picture panels: Levers and ramps; Two pulley arrangements; Related machine designs; Work and friction. Images are simplified models, not construction drawings, tool-use instructions or accessibility specifications. Arrows indicate directions unless a caption defines a numerical model. A machine can change force, distance, speed or direction; not every arrangement reduces effort force. Fixed and movable pulley arrangements differ, and supporting rope segments determine the ideal advantage. Ideal examples ignore friction and pulley weight; real input work is greater than useful output work when energy is dissipated. Friction changes mechanical energy into thermal energy rather than destroying it. Object pictures are observation examples. Build only the small, teacher-approved tabletop model described in this edition; do not lift a full water-cooler jug or use sharp tools for the activity.

history.title: The Deal
history.data:
## The Deal

A machine does not make you stronger. It changes how your strength gets used — and it always charges you for the favor.

There are six classic **simple machines**, and many everyday tools combine them.

A **lever** is a stiff bar that turns on a fixed point called a **fulcrum**. In one common arrangement, pushing down on one side of the fulcrum lifts the other side. A crowbar, a seesaw, a bottle opener, and the bones in your arm are all levers.

An **inclined plane** is a ramp. Walking a heavy box up a ramp takes less force than lifting it straight up — but you have to travel farther to get it to the same height.

A **wedge** is really an inclined plane that moves. An axe, a knife, a nail, and your front teeth all drive a thin edge into something and push it apart.

A **screw** is an inclined plane wrapped around a post. Look closely at the threads — that spiral is a ramp that has been rolled up. Turning the screw many times pulls it forward a small distance with great force.

A **wheel and axle** is a wheel fixed to a rod so they turn together. Doorknobs, steering wheels, and screwdrivers all use it. A tangential push at the wide outer edge can produce a larger force at the narrow axle; both turn through the same angle, while the rim travels farther.

A **pulley** is a wheel with a groove for a rope. A single fixed pulley changes pull direction. A movable pulley attached to a load can reduce the effort force. The ideal advantage depends on the rope segments supporting the moving load, not simply on the number of wheels.

Here is the ideal trade when a machine multiplies force: **less effort force means more effort distance.** Half the force requires twice the distance; a quarter requires four times the distance. Some arrangements instead change direction or increase movement speed. Without friction, input work equals output work.

Real machines also have **friction** and other losses, which convert some mechanical energy into thermal energy and other forms. These losses can be small or large. That is why rubbing your hands warms them and why machines need grease.

So when someone says a machine makes work easier, they mean something precise. A machine may reduce the required effort force, change its direction, or change speed. It cannot create energy. For the same useful task, losses make real input work greater than useful output work.

data.sourceExcerpt: Six classic simple machines are the lever, inclined plane, wedge, screw, wheel and axle, and pulley. When an ideal machine multiplies force, it trades longer effort travel for smaller effort force. Friction increases real input work.

essentialFacts: Lever: a stiff bar turning on a fulcrum.
Inclined plane: a ramp; a wedge is a ramp that moves; a screw is a ramp wrapped around a post.
Wheel and axle: a wheel fixed to a rod so they turn together.
Pulley: a grooved wheel with a rope that changes the direction or size of a pull.

history.title: Machine Check

questions.question: What is the fulcrum of a lever?
options: The heavy object being lifted
The fixed point the bar turns on
The force you apply
The long end of the bar
questions.correctAnswer: The fixed point the bar turns on

questions.question: A screw is really which simple machine in disguise?
options: A lever bent into a circle
Two pulleys joined together
An inclined plane wrapped around a post
A wedge with a wheel attached
questions.correctAnswer: An inclined plane wrapped around a post

questions.question: Why is pushing a heavy box up a ramp easier than lifting it straight up?
options: The box actually weighs less once it is on a ramp
Ramps work by removing friction from the surface entirely
Gravity stops pulling on objects that sit on a ramp
You use less force, but you travel a longer distance
questions.correctAnswer: You use less force, but you travel a longer distance

questions.question: An ideal machine lifts the same load using half the effort force. How far must the effort move compared with the load?
options: The effort must move twice as far as the load
Nothing at all, because machines add strength for free
The load you are lifting becomes twice as heavy
You must move the load twice as quickly to make up for it
questions.correctAnswer: The effort must move twice as far as the load

questions.question: What does friction do in every real machine?
options: Adds extra energy that increases the machine's total work
It only matters in machines that use wheels or axles
Converts some mechanical energy into thermal energy, increasing required input work
Builds up until it makes the machine stop working entirely
questions.correctAnswer: Converts some mechanical energy into thermal energy, increasing required input work

questions.question: Explain why a single pulley at the top of a flagpole is useful even though it does not reduce the force needed.
questions.expectedAnswer: It changes the DIRECTION of the pull. Instead of climbing the pole and lifting the flag upward, you can stand on the ground and pull down, which is much easier for a person's body even though the force is the same.

questions.question: Your friend says 'machines let you do less work.' Correct the statement precisely.
questions.expectedAnswer: For the same useful task, an ideal machine has equal input and output work. A force-multiplying arrangement reduces effort force by increasing effort distance. Other arrangements change direction or speed. Friction means real input work is greater than useful output work; energy is not destroyed.

reflections.text: Which simple machine do you use most in a normal day without thinking about it?

history.title: Machine Questions

data.question: Could ancient people really move those enormous stones? 🗿
data.answer: Yes, with ramps, levers, ropes, and enormous numbers of people. No lost technology is needed — simple machines plus organization explain the pyramids and Stonehenge, though archaeologists still debate the exact methods.

data.question: Is a bicycle a simple machine?
data.answer: It is a COMPOUND machine — several simple ones working together: wheels and axles, levers in the brakes and pedals, and screws holding it all in place.

data.question: Can a machine ever be 100% efficient? 🤔
data.answer: An ideal model can be 100% efficient. Ordinary real machines have friction and other losses, so useful output work is less than input work. Bearings and lubrication reduce these losses; their size depends on the machine.

data.question: Why is a knife sharp instead of blunt?
data.answer: A thin edge concentrates your force onto a tiny area, which is what makes a wedge work. The same push on a blunt edge is spread out and just squashes things.

data.question: Are my body parts machines?
data.answer: Genuinely, yes. Your forearm is a lever with the elbow as fulcrum, your jaw is a lever, and your teeth are wedges. Biology is full of simple machines.

data.question: Why do screws grip so much better than nails? 🔩
data.answer: The thread is a long ramp wrapped around the shaft, so turning it many times converts a small twisting force into a very strong pull — plus those threads bite into the material and resist pulling out.

data.title: Lift the Water Jug — Tabletop Model
data.instructions: Design and test a small tabletop model of a machine that could help lift a water jug. Use a sealed container with a total mass no greater than 250 grams as the model load. Raise it no more than 10 centimeters above a tray, with teacher approval. Do not lift a full water-cooler jug.
data.fitReason: The reading's claim that machines trade distance for force is easy to repeat and hard to feel. A design task with a real load makes students choose the trade and measure what it costs.

brief.context: A water cooler needs replacement jugs, but a full jug is too heavy for this classroom experiment. Model the problem using a sealed container no heavier than 250 grams, a short ruler or craft plank, blocks, string, small classroom pulleys and a spring scale marked in newtons. Keep the setup on a tray and the rise at 10 centimeters or less.
brief.audience: Your teacher and the students who refill the cooler
brief.drivingQuestion: Which approved tabletop machine lets us lift the same model load with less measured force, and how much farther does the effort travel?
brief.seedDirection: Start from the deal: if you want to pull with half the force, plan to move something twice as far. Which machine makes that trade in the space you have?
lockedLessonFacts: A lever turns about a fulcrum; its arm lengths affect its force and distance trade.
A longer frictionless ramp reduces force along the ramp for the same rise.
A fixed pulley changes direction; a movable pulley can multiply force through supporting rope segments.
In an ideal machine, input work equals output work.
Real losses convert mechanical energy to other forms, increasing the required input.
openQuestions: How does ramp length affect pull for the same height?
How do effort-arm and load-arm lengths compare?
How many rope segments support the moving load?
What difference between predicted and measured pull might friction explain?
stakeholders: Classmates observing from clear of the model
criteria: The same sealed model load rises the same small height in each comparison
Measure pull in newtons within the scale range and record effort travel and load rise
Predict the trade before testing, then compare prediction with evidence
Name the machine parts and explain where friction may affect the result
constraints: Total model-load mass is no more than 250 grams
Raise the model no more than 10 centimeters above a tray
Teacher must check supports, attachments and scale range before testing
Keep fingers clear; use no sharp tools and no full-size jug
Change only one feature between comparison trials
brief.deliverable: A labeled design drawing, a prediction (force before, force with machine, distance moved), a test table with spring-scale readings, and a short explanation of the trade using at least four glossary words.

parallelExample.context: A team needed to raise a small sealed model container onto a block.
parallelExample.move: They compared two ramps that reached the same 8-centimeter height. They pulled the same model steadily with a newton scale, recorded force and travel distance, and repeated each test. The longer ramp was predicted to need less pull; friction could change the measured values.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: The load and rise stayed constant while ramp length changed, making the comparison useful.

supports.frameStarter: We will use a ____ because it lets us ____. In exchange, we will have to ____.
frameChoices: A longer ramp reaching the same small platform
A lever with a longer effort arm than load arm
A teacher-approved movable pulley supported by two rope segments
A ramp with a fixed pulley to change pull direction
coachPrompts: Where in your design does the extra distance show up: rope, ramp, or lever arm?
What would happen to your force reading if you made the ramp shorter?
How will you show that the total work did not get smaller?

data.coachHint: Measure the pull with the scale before you use the machine and after. The difference is the trade; the extra distance is the price.
